title: Does Marriage Matter More Than We Thought? Challenging the Selection Narrative
gist: Harry Benson's PhD reanalysis of the UK Millennium Cohort Study challenges the dominant 'selection' view that marriage merely marks already-stable couples. Retaining the ~25% of families dropped for missing data and comparing eventually-married with never-married parents over 14 years, he finds selection explains only about half of the stability gap.

insights.claim: For more than 15 years the dominant view among family researchers has been that married parents stay together more because of who marries (selection), not because marriage itself makes a difference.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/familystudies/
insights.so_what: This consensus has shaped family policy and discouraged pro-marriage messaging.

insights.claim: Benson argues the selection narrative has discouraged politicians from saying anything positive about marriage, since it implies marriage is just a marker for couples destined to succeed.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/familystudies/
insights.so_what: Research framing directly influences policy on marriage incentives and family benefits.
insights.quote: discouraged politicians from saying much positive about marriage

insights.claim: Influential UK IFS studies from 2010-2013 concluded that after controlling for education, income, age and relationship quality, marriage explained little if any of the remaining difference in family stability.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/familystudies/
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific studies underpinning the UK policy consensus.
insights.locator: My PhD study began by replicating

insights.claim: Benson first replicated the UK IFS findings using the same Millennium Cohort Study sample and methods, obtaining almost the same headline results, so later differences stem from analysis choices, not data.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/familystudies/
insights.so_what: Replication-first design strengthens credibility of the revised result.

insights.claim: About one quarter of otherwise eligible families were excluded from the original studies due to missing data, and these were disproportionately couples who never married or later separated.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/familystudies/
insights.so_what: Complete-case analysis likely biased estimates toward making married and unmarried couples look alike.
insights.quote: The excluded quarter contained disproportionately more couples who never married or later separated.
insights.locator: My replication suggests that this mattered

insights.claim: Because missing data are rarely random and multiple imputation was well established by 2010, excluding incomplete cases risked biased estimates by dropping the most unstable families.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/familystudies/
insights.so_what: A general caution on survivorship-style bias in social-science evidence used for policy.

insights.claim: Around one quarter of parents classed as 'not married' at birth married within three years and more than one third within 14 years, so 'married vs. not-yet-married' comparisons understate marriage's long-term association with stability.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/familystudies/
insights.so_what: Misclassification of eventual marriers dilutes the measured marriage effect.

insights.claim: Extending follow-up to 14 years with 27 controls, adding back the missing-data quarter reduced selection's share of the stability gap from almost all to roughly two-thirds.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/familystudies/
insights.so_what: Shows one methodological fix alone materially shifts conclusions.
insights.locator: My PhD thesis then extended the analysis

insights.claim: Comparing parents who eventually married with those who never married over 14 years, selection explained only around half or less of the difference in union dissolution.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/familystudies/
insights.so_what: Implies marriage itself has a substantial independent association with family stability.
insights.quote: selection explained only around half or less of the difference in union dissolution

insights.claim: Benson concludes marriage has been substantially underestimated as a contributor to family stability, while acknowledging selection still matters.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/familystudies/
insights.so_what: Could shift policy debate toward supporting marriage as a stability lever.
insights.quote: Selection clearly matters. But marriage itself appears to have been substantially underestimated.

insights.claim: Education and economic situation matter less to union dissolution than many assume, while family background, parental separation, partnership history and relationship happiness matter more.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/familystudies/
insights.so_what: Challenges economic-only explanations of family instability.
insights.locator: My PhD dissertation does not claim

insights.claim: Even studies that do find a marriage effect beyond selection, such as Musick and Michelmore and Crossman et al., omit it from abstracts, so policymakers and journalists absorbing headlines entrench the selection view.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/familystudies/
insights.so_what: Headline-driven research consumption can lock in a conventional wisdom that the underlying data does not support.
insights.quote: relatively few readers study regression tables

insights.claim: Laurie DeRose, Brad Wilcox and colleagues (World Family Map) compared marrying vs. non-marrying parents over 12 years and also concluded marriage may meaningfully contribute to stability.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/familystudies/
insights.so_what: Independent corroboration of the revised view.

insights.claim: Three psychological mechanisms may let marriage create commitment: Stanley's 'deciding vs. sliding' theory, signal theory of marriage as a costly public commitment, and cognitive consistency after public vows.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/familystudies/
insights.so_what: Provides causal mechanisms for why the institution, not just the people, could matter.
insights.locator: The methodological findings point to a broader omission.

insights.claim: Benson argues researchers should shift from asking whether married couples were different beforehand to asking what happens to people when they marry, because marriage may help create commitment rather than merely reflect it.
insights.speaker: https://www.facebook.com/familystudies/
insights.so_what: Reframes the research agenda that informs family policy.
insights.quote: marriage may not simply reflect commitment. It may also help create it.
insights.locator: At the minimum, these theories suggest
